extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of scientific method, philosophers of science, researchers and advanced learners studying induction and definition
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for forming, naming, and defining general conceptions used in induction: how to observe, compare, classify, name, and define classes so as to support reliable generalization. Emphasizes appropriateness, clarity, and principles of definition for scientific inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of conception
rubrics_metrics.description: A conception is appropriate if it corresponds to a real agreement among the phenomena and helps toward the particular object of inquiry; appropriateness is relative to the purpose in view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: grouping animals by color produces legitimate conceptions but is inappropriate for studying anatomy or habits; grouping by skeleton-structure is more appropriate for those aims. Anti-pattern: selecting an agreement that does not extend to all cases of the phenomenon or that includes cases not belonging to the phenomenon (e.g., Aristotle's 'moving toward its own place' which omitted many spontaneous motions and included non-spontaneous ones).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity (determinate conception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceptions must be clear: we must know exactly in what the supposed agreement consists, having carefully observed and accurately remembered the distinguishing points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clear conception is determinate and invariant in use: never class things together without knowing why, and do not vary the connotation except consciously when knowledge advances. Requirements include habits of attentive observation, extensive experience, and an accurate memory. Anti-patterns: vague general feelings of resemblance without analysis; using names without precise connotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classes must be real (correspond to real distinctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: To ascertain general truths we must form classes that are genuinely classes—things included must really agree in certain particulars and differ from others in those particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a class is not a real class (no distinctive points of agreement), general propositions about it cannot be reliably established. Test by comparison and by checking that the purported common properties truly hold across the class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of classifications to the investigator's purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Even a clear and real class must comprise properties that are of primary importance for the theoretical or practical purpose at hand; classifications should be chosen to serve the inquiry's ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer properties that 'go deepest into the nature of the things' or are most closely connected to the specific property under investigation. Example: color-based classes are inadequate for structural/physiological questions. Scoring note: judge by usefulness toward the intended explanatory or practical goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of premature or dogmatic general conceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: General conceptions formed without thorough knowledge (Bacon's 'notiones temerè à rebus abstractæ') are inevitable but become impediments when permanently acquiesced in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Premature conceptions are acceptable as working hypotheses but are harmful if treated as final truths that resist replacement; watch for habitual misgrouping and refusal to reclassify despite better evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation and comparison as indispensable conditions of induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation and abstraction (comparison) are necessary preconditions for induction; there can be no induction where these are absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inductive inferences rely on bringing whole classes to view, comparing instances, and ascertaining uniformities. Poor or careless observation yields vague or false conceptions; rigorous, varied observation and comparison are required to justify generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activity and training of observational faculties (scientific imagination)
rubrics_metrics.description: The chance of hitting upon appropriate conceptions increases with the activity, facility, and store of relevant conceptions in the observer's mind (scientific imagination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mind well-trained in accurate observation and comparison, and stocked with relevant general conceptions, will perceive important agreements sooner and more reliably. Cultivate readiness to notice agreements and the imaginative faculty to conjecture plausible hidden resemblances when direct comparison fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of hypotheses/prior conceptions when comparison alone fails
rubrics_metrics.description: When simple comparison of phenomena fails to reveal the important agreement, prior conceptions or hypotheses (acquired elsewhere) may be legitimately invoked to suggest where to search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: searching for a lost object—if not seen, imagine possible hiding-places. Examples: invoking celestial mechanics concepts to discover planetary laws. Scoring note: hypotheses should prompt tests against facts; they are aids, not substitutes for evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming (general names) as an instrument of induction
rubrics_metrics.description: General names and propositions are essential instruments for recording, remembering, and applying the uniformities discovered by induction; without them we could not effectively reason about classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General names serve as artificial memory enabling the storage and retrieval of uniformities; they are not merely conveniences for dealing with many individuals but enable stating and communicating general propositions. Anti-pattern: reliance solely on proper names would preclude meaningful general assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every general name must have a fixed and precise meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: For language to serve the investigation of general truths, every general name must have a meaning steadily fixed and precisely determined (its connotation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vague terms (e.g., 'civilized', 'honor') which lack precise connotation cannot be subjected to correct induction. Fixing meaning is imperative for using names as instruments of thought and communication in science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition should respect and, where possible, align with existing usage
rubrics_metrics.description: When fixing the connotation of a term already in use, one should, so far as practicable, avail oneself of the associations already connected with the name and avoid meanings that conflict with received propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid definitions that demand radical revolutions in speech or render commonly accepted propositions false. The fixed connotation should agree with vague, fluctuating prior usage 'as far as it goes.' Practical constraint: social and linguistic continuity makes arbitrary redefinition undesirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions must be chosen on evidential and functional grounds, not arbitrarily
rubrics_metrics.description: To define a concrete name is to select among the common attributes of the denoted objects those that should constitute the connotation; this selection should be guided by experience and theory (choose attributes on which others depend or which are reliable marks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framing a good definition is often an inductive operation requiring comparison and may need improvement as knowledge advances. Prefer attributes that are well-known and those that serve as sure marks for inferring other properties. Scoring note: a good definition improves inferential power and explanatory depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explication of conceptions (unfolding) to resolve definitional disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: Contentious scientific debates often take the form of battles of definitions; but definitions derive importance from the propositions they aim to express, so explication must connect terms to the substantive propositions and evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When disputing definitions (e.g., measures of force, mineral species), seek the tacit propositions the definition is meant to express; the value of a definition is its role in expressing true or useful propositions. Practical approach: analyze which propositions the definition must preserve or enable.
